newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Dlr/yen vols slide as spot loses steam.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Dlr/yen vols slide as spot loses steam.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar/yen options slipped lower in U.S. trading as the spot dollar quickly lost steam after an initial rally following Sunday's Group of Seven meeting, dealers said.
Still, the market remained cautious despite the mostly benign comments from G7 monetary authorities, who appeared to be content with current exchange rates, traders said.
"It's a little spooky because you would have expected the dollar to jump higher if the G7 didn't try to lower it," said Masao Okada, chief options trader at Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank in New York.
The dollar did indeed test highs initially in Tokyo time, poking above 127.00 yen and pushing up one-month implied volatility by half a point to 9.7/10.0 percent.

However, the rally quickly fizzled out and one-month volatility recoiled to 8.4/8.6 percent by early U.S. afternoon. Traders said large selling by a U.S. investment bank in three-week options near the highs triggered a wave of selloffs.
"The long-term trend is still intact, but nobody's trying to drive it higher right now," said a trader at a European bank in Chicago.
There was also persistent selling in the six-month area by a British bank, which depressed the mid- to back-end of the curve, traders said.
Okada added that dealers' moves to trim their at-the-money hedge against their shorts in low-delta "wing" strikes tended to accelerate volatility declines when spot stayed steady.

As end-users buy low-delta options before an event, dealers become short in the "wing" strikes and hedge those positions with at-the-moneys. When spot barely moves after the event and volatilities start sliding, the value of the "wing" deteriorates quickly, making the at-the-money hedge too rich.
When volatilities go down, out-of-the-money options lose delta, and therefore gamma and vega, while characteristics of at-the-money options change very little as their delta stays at about 50.

Okada called this the "goma risk", noting that goma represented the rate of change in vega per incremental rise or fall in volatilities, while vega itself was the speed of change in premiums per movement in volatility.
Risk reversals, the cost of swapping equally low-delta puts and calls, slightly narrowed their skew for yen calls. One-month 25-delta was at 0.0/0.25 point favoring yen calls.
In dollar/mark options, the front end eroded a little after the initial spot rally stalled, but the back end was mostly steady.
One-month dollar/mark volatility was quoted at 8.8/9.0 percent, down from Friday's 9.0/9.2.
"At least dollar/mark made a new high," Okada said. The dollar touched a 37-month high of 1.7389 marks earlier in the day before pulling back.
The Chicago trader said the back end would eventually come under pressure, however, if gains in spot stayed as slow as they have been recently.
